t: Servant Leadership Is a Great Idea That Doesnt Really Work
q: With some notable workplace exceptions, servant leadership works better in theory than in practice.
The vast majority of enterprises, profit, and non-profit would implode under the guidance of a servant leader.
Servant leadership presumes others will operate in good faith and find the structure and support they need
Because servant leaders value consensus more than urgency and decisive action, opportunities are often lost
Examine an organization with a servant leader and you will likely see a lack of strategic alignment.
The best leaders are ALSO servant leaders. They support people while keeping their own ambitions and interests in check.
By putting the organization and the individual on equal footing, the best leaders are subservient in the right way.
x: Servant leadership alone tends to under-deliver on accountability and strategic alignment.

t: Break the Spell of the Tell
q: Team leaders push, prod, and cajole people to get them to act. Yet, people wait for instructions.
For leaders, TELL is the faster and most efficient way to get others to do what you want them to.
Leaders who vacillate between directing others and then giving them the freedom to act on their own confuse everyone
Breaking the pattern of TELL requires a tremendous amount of patience on everyone’s part.
Stepping back and watching people execute can be tremendously painful.
Once deprogrammed from the TELL, people regain the ability to act on their own, without waiting for instructions.

t: How To Become A Better Teacher Instantly
q: It’s to take responsibility for everything that happens in your classroom. Ownership. Duty. Blame. Onus. The buck stops with me. The whole nine.
Take responsibility anyway. For it all. It can be the best teaching decision you’ve ever made. As soon as you do it, as soon as you say, “It’s on me,” things will instantly begin to change.
You’ll stop complaining and being a victim. You’ll instead automatically look for solutions. Your disposition and character will also change.

Taking responsibility is leadership. Not many people are willing to do it because it’s hard and takes toughness. You have to stand on your own two feet, embrace uncertainty, and risk the fear of excellence .
Do it now before the start of a new school year. It’s a decision, nothing more. Go on. Walk to the edge. Close your eyes. And take the leap.
x: Taking full ownership of everything that happens in the classroom, regardless of circumstance, is framed as an instantly transformational decision.
Students remain responsible for their own behavior, but the teacher benefits from taking responsibility for outcomes anyway.

Linsin presents a single, uncomfortable but transformational idea: taking full ownership of everything that happens in one's classroom, regardless of circumstances like a difficult principal, an unwanted grade level, or…
Taking responsibility is described as an act of leadership requiring the courage to abandon excuses and risk uncertainty.
The piece closes with an extended metaphor of leaping off a ledge, urging readers to make the decision immediately, before the new school year begins.

t: 3 Misconceptions Of Effective Classroom Management anagement/
q: The only thing that needs to be strict is your adherence to your classroom management plan. As for where you place your boundaries, it’s up to you.
The idea that you have to be hard and severe while managing your classroom endures to this day. The truth is, a stern disposition is a waste of energy.
Good classroom management happens fast if you follow the core principles of SCM . Your confidence in what you’re doing is enough to communicate that your class is different.
When you set your behavior expectations in highly specific detail, whereby students feel the shock of excellence, they sit up straighter. They desire to be better.
You can and should expect impeccable behavior right now . There is no warming up. There is no room for doubt or excuses.
x: He clarifies that what needs to be strict is a teacher's adherence to their own plan, not the severity of the boundaries themselves, which can be set flexibly to match a teacher's preferences.

t: A Simple Way To Have Better Classroom Management Next Year
q: The way it works is to list the five most disruptive, annoying , and stressful misbehaviors you witnessed last school year.
Now, draw a line from each misbehavior to the rule it breaks. If you can’t do this, then you need to create another rule.
You see, whatever misbehavior you model—as in how not to behave —you’re less likely to get from your students.

It communicates in a way students understand why such misbehavior is wrong and how it tramples on the rights of others. In fact, if modeled explicitly and followed by your promise to hold your students accountable, they’re loathe to repeat it.

And because it comes at the beginning of the year, before they can engage in such behavior, they won’t be offended. You’re not poking fun at anyone personally. However, many will see themselves in the behavior.
x: A quick end-of-year exercise: list the five most disruptive misbehaviors from the past year and match each to an existing classroom rule, adding new rules as needed.
